outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 has settled or moved the question of whether infinitely many Cullen primes exist; the list of known classical Cullen prime indices is unchanged since 2009 (16 terms, largest 6679881), and every in-window prime record I found is a generalized Cullen prime in a base other than 2, which asks a different question.
problem_asks: Whether there are infinitely many positive integers n for which the Cullen number C_n = n·2ⁿ+1 is prime. One part: the infinitude of the set of Cullen primes. The statement names no other quantity, and does not ask about the prime-index case (whether some prime p has C_p prime), generalized bases n·bⁿ+1 with b other than 2, or the density of Cullen primes.

events.what_happened: Raphael M. Robinson showed that 141·2¹⁴¹+1 is prime, the first Cullen prime after Cullen's 1905 paper (Cullen had checked n up to 100 and Cunningham, 1906, n up to 200, finding 141 the only possible term up to 200). OEIS A005849 credits Robinson with a(2) and dates it 1958; a search snippet from the Riesel prime database gives 1957. I used 1958 from OEIS (opened), and the venue of Robinson's publication was not verified.
events.delivers: One finite instance: n = 141 gives a Cullen prime. Settles nothing about infinitude, since a single prime index does not move a claim about infinitely many.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many n give C_n prime.
events.directly_checkable: 141·2¹⁴¹+1 = 393050634124102232869567034555427371542904833, which is prime (value quoted in OEIS A050920 example, opened only as search snippet of that page).
events.direction: Finite instance of the family being asked about; neither supports nor cuts against infinitude.
events.object: The Cullen prime for n = 141: 141·2¹⁴¹+1, an explicit prime found by direct test.

events.what_happened: Christopher Hooley, in Applications of Sieve Methods to the Theory of Numbers (Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics 70, 1976), showed that the natural density of positive integers n for which C_n is prime is o(x). Wikipedia states this as almost all Cullen numbers are composite, citing Everest et al. (2003) p. 94. Hiromi Suyama later reworked the argument to cover n·2ⁿ+a+b, including Woodall numbers. I did not open Hooley's book or Suyama's paper; the statement is taken from the Wikipedia article (opened) and the 2026 Batte–Bravo–Luca introduction (opened), which both cite Hooley.
events.delivers: The set of n with C_n prime has natural density zero (the count up to x is o(x)). This restricts how many Cullen primes there can be in relative terms. It does not decide whether there are infinitely many, because a density-zero set can be infinite.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many n give C_n prime.

checked_by.qualification: Specialists in linear recurrence sequences; their book is the source Wikipedia cites for this statement
checked_by.what_they_did: Cite and restate the density result (per the Wikipedia citation). I did not open the book to confirm the page

events.direction: Partial result on the counting question: it says Cullen primes are rare in density but does not assert or deny the conjecture of infinitely many.

events.what_happened: Jon Grantham and Hester Graves, The abc Conjecture Implies That Only Finitely Many s-Cullen Numbers Are Repunits, arXiv:2009.04052 (identifier month September 2020; later published in the Journal of Integer Sequences, vol. 24 (2021), Article 21.5.3). The paper concerns the intersection of s-Cullen numbers with repunits, conditional on abc. Seen only as a search snippet and listing; I did not open the paper.
events.delivers: A conditional finiteness result for repunit s-Cullen numbers. A different question: it is about when a Cullen-type number is a repunit, not about when C_n is prime.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the question of infinitely many Cullen primes is not addressed.
events.direction: Different question (repunit intersection, conditional on abc); does not cut either way on prime values of C_n.

events.what_happened: Chris K. Caldwell, An Amazing Prime Heuristic, arXiv:2103.04483, first submitted 7 March 2021, v1 only, described as a book chapter (20 pages). The abstract (opened) says it develops a probabilistic heuristic and applies it to special prime forms; a search snippet says section 4.2 applies it to Cullen and Woodall primes, with predicted-versus-actual counts tabulated. The PDF was not readable with my tools, so I could not quote section 4.2 and the Cullen-specific content is unverified. Grantham–Graves and PrimePuzzles attribute to Caldwell the conjecture that infinitely many Cullen primes exist.
events.delivers: A heuristic argument, not a proof, supporting the conjecture that infinitely many Cullen primes exist. It delivers no rigorous statement about infinitude.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many n give C_n prime, rigorously.
events.doubts: A search snippet, attributed to a heuristic paper that is probably this one, says the data does not support the predicted count well for Cullen numbers, and that naive summing of probabilities overcounts. Unverified: I could not open section 4.2.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture of infinitely many Cullen primes heuristically; a heuristic is not a result on the question.

events.what_happened: Comments on PrimePuzzles problem pages about the prime-index case (whether some prime p gives C_p prime), which is a neighbouring question and not in this statement. On puzzle 1047, comments dated the week of 24–30 July 2021: Ken Wilke shows 3 divides C_p when p ≡ 1 (mod 6) and gives a mod-7 family; Simon Cavegn reports nothing found up to p = 397093; Emmanuel Vantieghem reports second-hand that all p < 10⁷ have been checked; Sebastian Martín Ruiz reports none up to p = 70657. On problem 50 (undated comments), Daniele Degiorgi and Farideh Firoozbakht record divisibility facts, including: if p+2 is prime then p+2 divides C_p. I re-derived this: 2^(p+2−1) ≡ 1 gives 2ᵖ ≡ 2⁻¹ and p ≡ −2 modulo p+2, so C_p ≡ 0.
events.revisions: Problem 50 comments are undated; date here is from puzzle 1047.
events.delivers: Divisibility facts and search ranges for the prime-index case of C_p. These bear on the neighbouring question of whether a Cullen prime has prime index. They do not touch whether infinitely many Cullen primes exist.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many n give C_n prime.
events.directly_checkable: The divisibility p+2 | C_p when p+2 is an odd prime can be checked by hand from Fermat's little theorem (done above).
events.doubts: Search-range claims (p < 10⁷, p ≤ 397093, p ≤ 70657) are comments, not published results; the p < 10⁷ claim is second-hand by its author's own account.
events.direction: Partial facts about a different sub-question (prime index); no effect on the infinitude question.

disputes.summary: Discovery credits for Cullen primes conflict. Riesel database (search snippet) gives Keller's four 1995 primes as found in 1984; OEIS A005849 dates them 1995. Robinson's n=141 is 1957 in the Riesel snippet and 1958 in OEIS. OEIS comments credit Gesker with 6328548; OEIS Extensions credit Blazek, May 2009.

A PrimePuzzles problem-50 contributor (Enoch Haga, undated) writes that Hooley's formula implies an infinite number of Cullen primes, and says the question is open. The density result (o(x)) does not imply infinitude, so the claim does not establish the conjecture. The page records the problem as open.

Known classical Cullen prime count: Batte–Bravo–Luca introduction says sixteen (HTML, opened), a search snippet says the PrimePages list has fifteen and omits 6328548 (not opened), and OEIS and Wikipedia list sixteen (opened).

summary: Across 39 web searches and about 20 page fetches (listed under search.places_checked), nothing since 26 January 2024 has settled or moved the infinitude question, and the open status is unchanged. Wikipedia (opened, 2026) still says 'Still, it is conjectured that there are infinitely many Cullen primes' with no citation, and PrimePages (opened) says it 'has been conjectured' and does not say known. OEIS A005849 (opened; last modified 11 October 2026, the date of this run) still lists 16 indices, the largest 6679881, so no new classical Cullen prime has appeared since 2009 as far as these sources show. The Batte–Bravo–Luca 2026 introduction agrees on sixteen. Every in-window prime record I found is a generalized Cullen prime n·bⁿ+1 with b other than 2: base 5 (Aug 2024), base 484 (Oct 2024, snippet only), base 294 (Nov 2024, snippet only), base 310 (Mar 2025, snippet only), base 355 search ranges (Mar–Apr 2025, snippet only), base 69 (16 April 2025, PrimeGrid, opened via PrimePages and Wikipedia), base 1001 (24 Aug 2025, opened), and base 30 (Apr 2026, opened via the Top 20 list). Under the scope rule these answer a different question, since a prime in base 69 does not bear on whether n·2ⁿ+1 is prime infinitely often. The one in-window arXiv paper on Cullen numbers, Batte–Bravo–Luca (arXiv 2605.23084, 21 May 2026), concerns membership of Cullen and Woodall numbers in Padovan and Perrin sequences, not primality. Li and Chen (Colloq. Math., online 18 November 2024) concern repunit generalized Cullen numbers, another question. I found no published claim, retraction, or Lean formalisation involving Cullen primes, and no later paper that treats the question as settled. Close calls: (1) the generalized-base discoveries could be read as showing that the Cullen family keeps producing primes, but I count them as a different question, as the scope rule requires. (2) Caldwell's 2021 heuristic supports infinitude but is not a result, and I could not open its section 4.2, so its Cullen-specific fit is unverified. (3) Hooley's density result is consistent with either answer; the PrimePuzzles claim that it implies infinitude is wrong as stated. (4) The prime-index sub-question is not in the statement. I recorded its partial facts, including the re-derived fact that p+2 divides C_p whenever p+2 is an odd prime, but none of them bears on the problem as stated. AI: no source I opened or found credits an AI system with any part of Cullen-prime mathematics, and no AI-involved record names Cullen numbers. The AI-and-primes news I found concerns other questions: a claimed GPT-5.6 prime-gap result (one secondary source, 36Kr, unverified; another source disputes one version, and the OpenAI-linked prime-gap bound is an unreviewed preprint per a tracker; none opened); an Anthropic claim on the Riemann zeta function; and the OEIS Open benchmark (Adamczewski, arXiv 2608.11941, 12 August 2026, opened), which mentions language models only in general and no Cullen conjecture. Six of the 39 searches were dedicated AI searches (queries 6, 17, 18, 25, 26, 39), with no Cullen hit. The classical PrimeGrid search status after 2015 is not established: MathWorld's 13,705,481 bound dates from November 2015 and I could not open PrimeGrid or Riesel's current pages (HTTP 503).
competing_reading: The strongest reading against 'nothing happened' is that the Cullen family is actively searched: PrimeGrid runs both the classical and generalized Cullen searches, and in the window it produced a record-size generalized prime (base 69, April 2025), a 797,119-digit proven prime (base 1001, August 2025), and a base-30 entry in the Top 20 (April 2026). A reader who weights search activity over the question as stated could count these as progress on the family. The scope rule rejects that: each concerns b ≠ 2, and finitely many instances in other bases do not change whether infinitely many n·2ⁿ+1 are prime. A second reading treats Caldwell's heuristic or Hooley's density result as bearing on infinitude. Neither moves the question, since a heuristic is not a result and a density-zero set can still be infinite.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that infinitely many n give n·2ⁿ+1 prime, or a proof that only finitely many do, published or posted and checked by specialists; none exists in any source I could reach as of 11 October 2026. Short of that: the current PrimeGrid classical Cullen search status and bound (the PrimeGrid and Riesel pages returned HTTP 503), the Stănică–Luca 2003 text on the composite-below-412000 claim (the PDF was unreadable with my tools), and the full text of Caldwell's section 4.2 (the PDF was unreadable). Any new classical Cullen index after 6679881 in OEIS A005849 would also be a direct event.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether infinitely many n make n·2ⁿ+1 prime. Each individual classical Cullen prime and the 2015 search range is a finite check, so those are instances. Every post-snapshot event is about a different question: primes of the form n·bⁿ+1 with b ≠ 2, repunit intersections, or membership in Padovan/Perrin sequences. All of those are variants. Hooley's density-zero theorem was the closest call. It does limit how many Cullen primes there can be, but it says nothing about whether there are infinitely many, so it neither settles nor bounds the question as asked. I scored it variant rather than bound, and since it predates the snapshot and is not resolved, the choice does not change the outcome. Caldwell's heuristic is not a result, so it is none. No AI system is credited anywhere.
judgement.doubts: Several generalized-base entries rest only on search snippets. They are variants either way. The current status of PrimeGrid's classical Cullen search was not established.
